title: The jathedar

cards: A voice needs a mouth. Yesterday the Akal Takht spoke for the panth, but a building can't read a letter aloud, sign it, or stand on the steps while the sangat listens. Somebody does that.
In news from Punjab the title turns up just before a name: Jathedar. It can sound like a rank in an army, or the head of a church. It isn't quite either.
The word has a smaller, everyday meaning too, and that meaning still sits inside the title.

teach.b: Start with the smaller word. A jatha is a band of Sikhs moving together for a purpose: a group of volunteers, a company of riders, a party of marchers, a kirtan group traveling from town to town.

The jathedar is the one who leads the jatha. This path has met that use already, in the bands of the Khalsa's hard years and the jathas of the gurdwara reform movement, walking out together, unarmed, toward the shrines.
Each of the Takhts has a jathedar, the person who heads it. The Jathedar of the Akal Takht is the one people hear about, because edicts for the whole panth go out from there.
A jathedar presides over the Takht's business, reads out its hukamnamas, and can summon Sikhs to answer before it. So: a leader of a moving band, and the head of a seat that doesn't move.

teach.h: THE BAND BECOMES THE WHOLE PANTH.
teach.b: Some readers hear the first inside the second: the jathedar of a Takht still leads a jatha, only now the band is the whole panth, and the job is to keep it moving together. Then a caution, so the title isn't misheard.
A jathedar is not a pope and not a Guru. Sikhs say the Guru is the Granth and the Panth, which this path met a few days ago.

teach.h: A SERVANT OF THE TAKHT, NOT A GURU.
teach.b: The jathedar serves the Takht; the Takht doesn't belong to the jathedar.
How jathedars are appointed is a live question among Sikhs, argued in good faith. But whoever holds the seat holds the same task.

how: Each Takht has a jathedar who heads it; the Jathedar of the Akal Takht presides over its business and reads out its hukamnamas to the panth.

o: the leader of a band of Sikhs, or the head of a Takht
the reader who opens the Granth each morning
a Guru chosen by vote to lead the whole community

games.why: the jathedar presides over the Takht's business and reads out its edicts, as a servant of the Takht, not its owner.

practice: Think of the best leader of a small band you've ever been part of, a coach, a shift manager, an older cousin on a road trip, and find one thing they did that kept everyone moving together.
Maybe they walked at the pace of the slowest, or spoke last; hold that one thing, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Jathedar. The leader of a jatha, a band of Sikhs, and the title of the person who heads each of the Takhts. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: the leader of a jatha, a band; also the title of a Takht's head.
